atoms.a:
Social credit system

The government affords or deducts social points according to each citizen’s behaviour. For example, citizens can gain points by praising the government on social media, while criticising the government loses them points. High social credit brings benefits, such as easier access to housing, while lower credit can lead to restrictions.

atoms.text: Parts of the social credit system are already being implemented in some Chinese cities. China's social credit systems are made up of multiple experiments rather than a single nation-wide system.

atoms.a:
Social castes

At birth, the government places every citizen into a predefined social category that determines education, career paths, and living conditions. Movement between categories is nearly impossible. The system is justified as a way to maintain stability and efficiency, ensuring everyone has a clearly defined role in society.

atoms.text: In the novel Brave New World (1932) by Aldous Huxley, people are artificially produced to fit into specific social and intellectual roles using genetic engineering.

Although Brave New World is an extreme example, some elements are similar to our reality. A child’s future opportunities are already strongly influenced by factors such as income and (dis)ability. While not formally assigned, social classes can become very fixed in practice.

atoms.a:
Algorithmic sentencing

In some courts, artificial intelligence analyses evidence, past records, and behavioural data to recommend sentences for minor criminal offences. The AI's suggestion is presented as statistically more reliable than human judgement.

atoms.text: Algorithmic tools are already used in some court systems to support decisions about sentencing or parole by estimating how likely a person is to reoffend based on statistical data. One example is COMPAS, used in the United States. However, these tools do not replace judges, and their use is highly controversial due to concerns about bias in the underlying data.

atoms.b: Many ((governments --countries))—real or fictional—justify their policies by claiming they will make life safer, more ((stable --dangerous)), or more efficient. Algorithmic sentencing, social credit scores, or ((fixed --flexible)) social roles are often justified as ways to reduce crime, reward good behaviour, or create ((social --digital)) stability. However, they also raise an important question: how much ((freedom --technology)) are we willing to give up in exchange for greater ((security --profit))?

Dystopian fiction encourages us to question whether the promise of ((security --danger)) can be used to justify surveillance, ((discrimination --equality)), or restrictions on personal freedom and individuality. It reminds us that protecting society should not come at the cost of fundamental rights and ((individual --collective)) autonomy.
